INTRODUCTION
"Democratic recession" - as defined by more regression than progression in countries characterized by
full or partial liberal democracy - is now approaching its 17th year.' While the exact number of years
may differ among observers and institutions, the increase in the number of instances of democratic
backsliding is, forthe most part, universallyacknowledged and undeniable. Nevertheless, there are some
"democratic openings" - or opportunities in which authoritarian, hybrid, or other non-democratic
regimes experience some movement, often unexpected, toward political liberalization and democratic
advances (countries in which gains for liberal democracy either outweigh losses or at least mitigate them
to some degree). For the United States Agency for International Development's (USAID) commitments
to democracy, human rights, and governance (DRG), identifying and predicting such democratic
openings would be important. It would suggest where investments of scarce DRG resources might yield
the greatest returns and realization of key development outcomes.
Employing a methodology designed and developed under the USAID-funded Swift Enterprise and
Grounded Analytics (SEGA) task order, awarded to DevTech Systems under the AS IV IDIQ, this report
provides a list of countries who may be, or are likely to, experiencing a democratic opening for USAID's
consideration. The methodology itself, provides a rigorous basis for such predictions and investments
based on hard, quantitative data complemented by a qualitative review of those data centered on six
primary factors and four less-critical but still important factors to consider. This methodology was
designed to be used by operating units—whether missions, regional bureaus or other Washington units
like the DRG Center—to evaluate the countries most likely as well as those unlikely to experience a
democratic opening in the foreseeable future. USAID can then decide on this basis and other
considerations where democracy investments are most likely to bear democratic results. The conclusions
will be imperfect at best but better than random forecasts. Moreover, correct predictions of
democratic openings hardly mean correct predictions of democratic successes and consolidations to
follow the openings.
Democratic openings may fail to mature and often do; in fact, the vast majority don't succeed and even
backslide. Even when they crystallize initially, they may stall or relapse. For example, widespread
expectations for a more democratic future in Tunisia, Algeria and Sudan, all supported by "data", have
soured. Similarly, early confidence in a democratic future for Bulgaria, Romania, and the countries of the
so-called "color revolutions" has been disappointing, notwithstanding their membership in and support
by the European Union, one of the most important inducements for democratic consolidation in those
countries. Consequently, the attempt outlined in this report should be taken with appropriate caution.
That caution does not obviate the attempt. It places the attempt in an appropriate analytical context for
those who advocate for and are charged with achieving results from democracy assistance.
DEMOCRATIC OPENINGS: DEFINITIONS AND PATHWAYS
Under the early textbook definition of a democratic opening, authoritarian regimes are most commonly
replaced quickly after a traumatic event like the death of the autocrat; a free competitive election with

surprising results; the adoption of a new constitution guaranteeing democracy and human rights by an
apparently regime-controlled parliament; or when a heretofore captured judiciary uncharacteristically
and often precipitously issues a decision that undermines the regime. Early examples of democracy
replacing existing authoritarian regimes can be traced back to the decolonialization and independence
movements in Africa, for example in Kenya, Uganda, and Nigeria, although they resulted in short-lived
democracies. Initially many thought that the Cuban revolution of 1959 grounded on the military victory
led by Fidel Castro would take a similar course except that Castro and his entourage were really, not
just rhetorically Communists, so it was followed by a Leninist dictatorship rather than a liberal
democracy-
Today, leading textbook examples of a democratic opening include the 1974 coup d'état by leftist miliary
officers in Portugal and the Spanish transition of 1975-78 - both examples from what Samuel Huntington
has defined as the Third Wave of democratic openings. 2 The November 1975 death of Spain's autocratic
leader, Francisco Franco, who ruled for 35 years through the fascist period and was an erstwhile ally of
Hitler, launched a new, democratic dispensation. With the support of King Juan Carlos, the military
dictatorship was replaced by a democratically elected parliament and the (now) constitutional monarchy.
The coup in Portugal was supported by an unanticipated popular campaign led by Portuguese citizen
refugees returning from Portugal's recently liberated African colonies.
Following these examples, the world watched as other democratic openings emerged across the globe.
In Asia, the 1986 Philippine opening replaced dictator Ferdinand Marcos based on massive "People
Power" popular demonstrations and the support of Cardinal Jaime Sin and, as the coup de grace,
withdrawal of U.S. support for Marcos by President Ronald Reagan. Marcos fled into exile and was
replaced in competitive elections by Corazon Aquino, wife of Marcos' long-time but assassinated
adversary, Benigno Aquino Jr. The ensuing period of liberal democracy arguably ended with the election
in 2016 of Rodrigo Duterte who ushered in a democratic regression to authoritarian rule. The most
dramatic democratic openings throughout Central Europe began with the 1989 collapse of party and
government discipline in East Germany, Poland, Hungary, and Czechoslovakia when the Soviet Union
unexpectedly decided not to intervene against a flow of exiles to the west or crush the large anti-regime
demonstrations. Those openings were followed by democratic openings in Bulgaria, Romania and the
Baltic countries of Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania.
For USAID purposes, however, a broader definition of democratic openings provides more common
and therefore more useful examples. A democratic opening need not depend on a specific traumatic
event or campaign but rather on a less singular and more gradual opening of political, economic and
social space over a longer period of time. As per capita income and the "mini" political and civil society
openings increase - as a middle-class forms and enlarges (both in numbers and in influence) - as
educational levels increase - as the pressure for a rule of law (initially often for contractual certainty
even for the regime's state-owned enterprises) - and as the desire for democracy swells (often when
the number citizens with access to broadcast, cable, and internet outlets grows); the nature of the
political and economic character of society can become more open and (potentially) democratic.

Press: 1991).

Regrettably, despite these democratic openings, whether traumatic or more gradual, they do not lock in
the democratic trajectories one would hope for. As Huntington predicted based on the earlier
democratic waves, the third wave of democratization (beginning in the mid-1970s with Portugal and
Spain and ending with the democratic regressions beginning in 2006), democratizations are not secure
indefinitely. Rather, authoritarians can make a comeback along with democratic reversals, backsliding, or,
in the current vocabulary, democratic recessions or regressions. The most obvious examples are the
countries of "the Arab Spring" where the past decade provides numerous illustrations of democratic
openings gone tragically wrong. In three cases - Syria, Yemen and Libya - the democratic potential
associated with the 2011 upheavals gave way to civil wars that triggered unprecedented human suffering
and further destabilized the entire region. In Egypt, the euphoria of the 2011 uprising was quickly
replaced with debilitating polarization, chaos, and, in July 2013, a military coup that yielded a far more
brutal form of authoritarianism than that once associated with the Mubarak regime. As for Tunisia, once
heralded as the Arab Spring's lone success story, it has regressed into one-man rule since July 202l,
after producing ten ineffective governments spanning a decade. To this end, this report presents the
inaugural application of the democratic opening methodology, and the results thereof, counting for both
the traumatic and the gradual paths of democratic openings. However, it is important to note that the
methodology itself does not deal with the contours or dynamics of democratic regressions.
DEMOCRATIC OPENINGS: STRUCTURAL FACTORS
Both recent and older history, including these examples, demonstrates that only a fraction of countries
that experience a "democratic opening" or "democratic trends" eventually transition to a democratic
regime. Based on historical evidence, long-term structural factors have repeatedly facilitated or,
conversely, proven to be a powerful impediment to such transition. These factors have become clearer
in the literature on democratization since Samuel Huntington's seminal 199l Third Wave book. In its
early years, approximately from the late 1980s through the early 2000s, that literature reflected
considerable optimism regarding the ability to take advantage of "windows of democratic opportunity"
or "democratic breakthroughs" and build lasting democracies out of them -- even in the absence of the
socioeconomic and other conditions that earlier generations of scholars had tended to see as essential
to the success of democracy. Indeed, the tendency to downplay structural impediments to democracy,
and the belief that democracy could strike roots even in terrain that seemed deeply unfavorable to it,
was pervasive in writing on democratization from the early 1990s through the early 2000s. Underlying
that optimism was the assumption that democracy could be "willed" and structural obstacles could be
overcome through "elite pacts," and, more generally, through proper political engineering and
institutional design.
Reality, and specifically the spate of democratic reversals experienced by many new democracies in the
past two decades, forced a reconsideration of that earlier optimism. There now exists far greater
skepticism about the ability of democracy to survive in the face of hostile structural conditions. For the
same reason, there is a consensus that the "transition literature" of the 1990s had been far too
dismissive of the extent to which such adverse conditions present powerful impediments to sustaining
democratic momentum, let alone to building actual democracies. In short, the new consensus is that
when it comes to democracy's prospects, long-term socioeconomic and political factors cannot be
ignored or wished away, and that they certainly should not be discounted as they so often were two or
three decades ago.

DEMOCRATIC OPENING
METHODOLOGY: AN OVERVIEW
The democratic opening list is based upon a methodology designed to recognize a democratic opening,
by analyzing the probability of its success or failure to ripen into a democracy. The methodology
employed a two-step, mixed methods approach, drawing on quantitative and qualitative approaches. A
brief overview of the methodology follows. For an in-depth discussion of the methodology, please refer
to Annex D.
STEP ONE: QUANTITATIVE COMPONENT
The first step of the methodology involves an in-depth analysis of rigorously accrued and available
quantitative data on democratic openings. The team considered several quantitative indices, including
Freedom House's Freedom in the World; the University of Gothenburg's Variety of Democracy (V-
Dem) Indices; and, the Economist Intelligence Unit's Democracy Index. In collaboration with USAID's
DRG Office, the team concluded that V-Dem—an on-going international attempt—would be the best fit
for the quantitative approach to democratic openings. Several of V-Dem's indicators represent the most
rigorous, detailed, and data-driven efforts to quantify democratic dynamics globally. Their application
constitutes Step One, the Quantitative Component, of the methodology. In particular, V-Dem's
Democratic Spaces Barometer (DemSpace) index—an annual index of democratic performance and
potential—combined with V-Dem's Liberal Democracy Index (LDI) and its V-Forecast Project. The
combined score of these indices is intended to predict democratic openings, from the most promising to
the least promising countries. The results of Step One, the complete ranking of nearly 170 countries,
can be found in Annex A.
STEP TWO: QUALITATIVE COMPONENT
Quantitative data and indices based on these datasets are not, by themselves, as reliable a source of
information as they would be if tempered by deep personal experience with the countries and the
interpretations that experience and insight brings to the analysis. Out of the many qualitative elements
that can affect a democratic opening, a parsimonious six— (I) per capita income; (2) government
performance and effectiveness; (3) the salience of ethnic religious and other identity divisions; (4)
dependency on primary commodities and exports and presence of a rentier state; (5) geopolitical and
regional influences; and (6) historical legacies-—are likely to have the most effect. In addition, are four
less-critical but still important factors to consider: (I) caliber of leadership; (2) the size and autonomy of
the middle class; (3) the level of party-system internalization; and (4) governance functions performed by
non-government entities. There are many other qualitative factors that could and often do affect
democratic openings, but the SEGA team has identified these as the most efficacious and significant for
analysts to consider in order to come to timely, practical conclusions. The results of Step Two, the
qualitative results, can be found in Annex B.

DATA ANALYSIS AND CALCULATING GLOBAL RANKINGS
Each component brings different insights to the selection process, and each approach can help
compensate for the blind spots of the other. The quantitative approach leverages information about
dozens or hundreds of variables capturing the experiences of almost all countries over many years. It
thus reveals general tendencies that can help rule out many countries that are unlikely to satisfy the
criteria. Of the several V-Dem products, the methodology uses forecasts by DemSpace along with LDI,
to narrow the list to 26 most likely countries, which reduces the workload in the qualitative stage.
The qualitative approach consists of deliberation by USAID or outside country and regional experts.3
They are designed to bring to the process deep, nuanced, and up-to-date knowledge of the countries on
the initial list produced by the quantitative step, as well as familiarity with theories of democratization.
Their understanding refines the analysis, ruling out forecasted openings that have already failed, openings
that are unlikely to take place or to last, and selecting cases for which forecasts of a successful, lasting
opening are credible.
Together, the two steps in the methodology provide a coherent, data-based process for recognizing
actual and potential democratic openings, ordering them by probability, and then applying a qualitative
filter to decide the best candidates for assistance. The report thus, constitutes a judicious, practical,
realistic, evenhanded albeit indeterminate attempt to implement a methodology designed to predict
democratic openings and point USAID assistance to the countries most likely in an uncertain world to
yield successful democratic openings.

BRIEF ANALYSIS OF SOMEWHAT LIKELY COUNTRIES
BRAZIL
The presidential elections which took place this year in Brazil have created a possible tipping point for
the country and a strong foundation for a democratic opening. Former president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva
won the run-off election on October 30, 2022, and a Lula presidency is likely to move Brazil back
toward a higher level of liberal democracy. On November I, 2022, President Jair Bolsonaro agreed to a
transition of power allowing the whole of the Brazilian governmental bureaucracy to begin preparing for
the da Silva administration.
COLOMBIA
Colombia, while democratic already, is not one of the most democratic countries in the hemisphere, and
it seems to be on the cusp of significant reforms, creating space for a domestic opening toward greater
democracy. Despite the negative impacts of neighboring Venezuela's economic collapse on Colombia,
the economy remains stable, the governmental bureaucracy remains competent and capable, and the
education system remains fairly good and accessible to the middle class. Furthermore, the new
president, Gustavo Petro, has an ambitious agenda to promote "total peace" through negotiations and
democracy, and he is backed by a two-thirds majority coalition in Congress.
ARMENIA
Armenia is at a critical juncture politically, a juncture that has created the potential for a democratic
opening. Since the Velvet Revolution of 2018, the Government of Armenia has taken steps to fight
corruption, enhance the integrity of the judicial system, and improve transparency in government
operations, but results have been slow to materialize. Pro-Russian, anti-democratic forces remain
politically strong but the pro-Western, pro-democratic forces have a good chance of prevailing. Armenia
demonstrates, however, that the struggle between autocracy and democracy does not always align
neatly with that which pits pro-Western forces against their opponents. Still, the challenge of solidifying

MALAYSIA
Between Malaysian independence in 1963 and the general election of 2018, a single party (a consortium
of a major Malay party and two junior Chinese and Indian parties) held unbroken political power. The
defeat of that party in 2018—in large part because of mammoth corruption under the ruling party,
especially of its prime minister now convicted of stealing hundreds of thousands of dollars from the
national wealth fund (and now in prison)—by a loose collection of parties, the ensuing serious electoral
competition, and better, less corrupt governance has created a moment where an opening for a true
democracy in Malaysia may be possible.. The future of a sustained democratic opening hinges in part on
whether economic and other social issues will trump ethnic/religious communalism in the national
political discussions, elections, and public policy and also on whether the previous 1963-2018 ruling
party returns to power after the next general elections.
DOMINICAN REPUBLIC
The Dominican Republic has lurched intermittently and awkwardly toward greater democracy and
possesses an environment conducive to achieving a democratic opening through fostering marginal
improvements. Governmental corruption as well as the marginalization and persecution of ethnic and
other minority groups remain strong disadvantages for a sustained democratic opening in the Dominican
Republic. However, the electoral process is relatively free and fair with strong participation from
citizens, which creates opportunities for a democratic opening.

violence and legitimacy and is unable to protect life and property across the country's large, often

effective policy design and implementation. For decades, the state has been oriented far more toward
donors, and toward collecting the rents associated with foreign assistance, than toward the population it
is supposed to serve. Viewed by Malians as corrupt, incompetent, predatory, or absent, the Malian state
is devoid of political legitimacy and does not command true political authority, a prerequisite for state
effectiveness.

This methodology is designed to recognize a democratic opening, by analyzing the probability of its
success or failure to ripen into a democracy, and the steps which assistance might play in improving the
chance of success. The methodology employs a two-step, mixed methods approach, drawing on
quantitative and qualitative approaches.
STEP ONE: QUANTITATIVE COMPONENT
The first step of the methodology involves an in-depth analysis of rigorously accrued and available
quantitative data on democratic openings. The team considered several quantitative indices, including
Freedom House's Freedom in the World; the University of Gothenburg's Variety of Democracy (V-
Dem) Indices; and, the Economist Intelligence Unit's Democracy Index. In collaboration with USAID's
Office of Democracy, Human Rights and Governance, the team concluded that V-Dem—an on-going
international attemptwould be the best fit for the quantitative approach to and recommendations for
assisting democratic openings. Several of V-Dem's indicators represent the most rigorous, detailed, and
data-driven efforts to quantify democratic dynamics globally. Their application constitutes Step One, the
Quantitative Component, of the methodology. In particular, V-Dem's Democratic Spaces Barometer
(DemSpace) index—an annual index of democratic performance and potential—combined with V-Dem's
Liberal Democracy Index (LDI) and its V-Forecast Project. The combined score of these indices is
intended to predict democratic openings, from the most promising to the least promising countries. The
first part of this methodology, Step One, covers the quantitative approach to recognizing and (to some
extent) predicting democratic openings in the nearly 170 countries included in the DemSpace index.
STEP TWO: QUALITATIVE COMPONENT
Quantitative data and indices based on these datasets are not, by themselves, as reliable a source of
information as they would be if tempered by deep personal experience with the countries and the
interpretations that experience and insight brings to the analysis. Out of the many qualitative elements
that can affect a democratic opening and its path, a parsimonious six-(1) per capita income; (2)
government performance and effectiveness; (3) the salience of ethnic religious and other identity
divisions; (4) dependency on primary commodities and exports and presence of a rentier state; (5)
geopolitical and regional influences; and (6) historical legacies—are likely to have the most effect. In
addition, are four less-critical but still important factors to consider: (I) caliber of leadership; (2) the size
and autonomy of the middle class; (3) the level of party-system internalization; and (4) governance
functions performed by non-government entities. To repeat, there are many other qualitative factors
that could and often do affect democratic openings, but analysts need a parsimonious list with the most
efficacious and significant ones in order to come to timely, practical conclusions.
DATA ANALYSIS AND CALCULATING GLOBAL RANKINGS
Each component brings different insights to the selection process, and each approach can help
compensate for the blind spots of the other. The quantitative approach leverages information about
dozens or hundreds of variables capturing the experiences of almost all countries over many years. It

ABOUT POLITICAL FORECASTING
In 2005, the political psychologist Philip Tetlock provided data and an analysis to support the view that
experts on politics were unable to forecast the occurrence of major political events in the near future
more than half of the time, i.e., no better than chance.62 They tend to over-extrapolate from the past,
rely on incomplete knowledge, use general theories or ideologies to fill in what they don't know, and
make logical errors about probabilities.
However, Tetlock has also demonstrated that there are "superforecasters" who can learn to do better
than chance. They have a keen interest in understanding the mechanism behind things, as opposed to
just getting accurate forecasts without knowing why. They question their line of reasoning. They are
willing to test new ideas. They never settle on one and only one forecasting mechanism, but rather
remain in a "perpetual beta" mode, realizing that life, as well as the world around them, is complex, that
nothing is for certain, that everything is constantly evolving. Moreover, they are well aware of the
fallacies and tricks that the mind can play on us to "make something look certain", leading to the
temptation to come to the "obvious" conclusion too quickly without second guessing it, and re-analyzing
the evidence that is presented over and over again. 63 More recently, he has reported that teams of
trained superforecasters can utilize "the wisdom of crowds" to do even better, but only if they can
manage to process strong disagreements and not succumb to groupthink. 64 However, even teams of
superforecasters are far from perfect, and do little better than chance when forecasting events more
than two years into the future.
In recent years, computational researchers have developed machine learning methods that automate
some of the principles of superforecasting. They have no preconceived theory; they examine hundreds
of variables in hundreds of thousands of combinations. They test randomly generated hypotheses on
vast amounts of data; they are immune to logical fallacies. Google, Amazon, supermarket chains, and
many other companies use these methods to predict what individual consumers are searching for and
what they are inclined to buy, and they have been fantastically successful at it.
Still, adapting such models for predicting major political events such as democratic openings introduces
special challenges. Many of the relevant factors are unmeasurable; the models are tethered to past data
in a world in constant flux; and events can hinge on seemingly random decisions made by individual
leaders. As a result, although machine learning models can outperform experts, they still have had only
modest success at predicting future political events. This is a good reason to pair computational
forecasts with a second stage in which country or regional experts can use qualitative information to
assess the plausibility of such predictions.
Another disadvantage of machine-learning forecasts is that they do not provide reasons for their
predictions, and it is basically impossible to ascertain the reasons after the fact. They predict that a
country will or will not become more democratic but not why. Consequently, they will not, on their
own and without more, give USAID sufficient guidelines for selecting promising cases in the future. This

Unlike the other V-Forecast project "Predicting Adverse Regime Transitions" (PART), DemSpace does

Alternative Approaches
An alternative forecasting approach is possible, but would require much more work in-house, and it has
not been validated. Rather than forecasting any opening of at least a small size, with uncertainty
expressed as the probability of the opening (as DemSpace does), USAID staff could attempt to forecast
the size of the opening, with uncertainty expressed as a range of sizes the opening could take. This
alternative might be considered "modeling magnitudes" vs. "modeling probabilities." Both approaches
are rather agnostic about what the true model is and yield few if any conclusions about why openings
happen. However, either approach can incorporate variables that are believed to be good predictors
and that may in fact improve the forecasts. These predictors tend to be useful for some countries or
years but not for others; but that is not the goal. Collectively, the predictors serve as a kind of Swiss
army knife: a multi-functional tool with some components useful for many situations and other tools
with more specialized uses. Since this approach is not likely to be adopted, it is explained more fully only
in Annex D.

STEP TWO: THE QUALITATIVE COMPONENT
From the perspective of the methodology, consideration of the factors introduced below would come
into play during the second phase of the two-stage methodology and analytical process. The second
stage, involving qualitative analysis, would enable decisionmakers at USAID to narrow down further a
preliminary list ("List A", please refer to Table I above) of countries featuring a promising "democratic
opening" or encouraging "democratic trends." List A would be produced through Step One. Drawing
on what is known about the structural conditions that shape prospects for turning a promising
democratic opening into a consolidated democracy, Step Two would identify from List A, a smaller
number of countries with a better than random chance of sustaining momentum toward democracy.
Countries with democratization potential -- as identified through Step One, by relying on mostly
statistical data -- but that exhibit hostile structural conditions (as determined through Step Two's more
granular, qualitative analysis) would be eliminated from, or downgraded on, the final, shorter list, on the
ground that they display "structural disadvantages" that mitigate against successful democratization.
The structural conditions introduced below, therefore, may be approached as a filter through which List
A would have to pass to create List B. Unlike List A, produced in Step One through largely quantitative
analysis relying on V-Dem data, List B would result from a process (Step Two) involving mostly
qualitative analysis. The analysis in question would require that those tasked with it possess both
specific country/regional expertise and, as importantly, familiarity with comparative analysis of
democratizing countries. 73
For the sake of parsimony, an effort was made to select only those structural conditions that scholars,
relying on empirical analysis of both contemporary and older trends in democratization, consistently
have found to be decisive for turning democratic potential into democratic reality -- or, conversely, for
thwarting the ability of a democratic opening to evolve into more sustained democratic momentum.
These factors, therefore, may be approached as "enabling" or "disabling" structural conditions -- as
"structural advantages" or "structural disadvantages" -- depending on how they play out in the country
being examined. 74 They consist of the following.
• Factor One: Per capita income (GDP per capita)
• Factor Two: Government Performance and Effectiveness

HOW IT MATTERS MOST: THE CONSEQUENTIAL IMPACT OF MULTIPLE STRUCTURAL ADVANGAGES
OR DISADVANTAGES
As noted earlier, structural conditions matter most to a country's democratization prospects not
individually, but when they are considered as a whole. Whether a country enjoys "multiple structural
advantages," or, conversely, whether is suffers from "multiple structural disadvantages," is critical.97 One
key finding from the comparative literature is that democratization is extremely likely to falter in
countries that suffer from several structural disadvantages. Put differently, the greater the number of
structural disadvantages at play, the exponentially less likely it becomes that a democratic opening will
result in a democratic transition. That is the case, in part, because where several structural
disadvantages are involved, each thwarts democracy not just on its own, but because it also tends to
exacerbate the others. Revealingly, poor, ethnically diverse, and badly governed societies are rare among
democracies. 98 Noticeably as well, as Larry Diamond noted a decade ago, countries that initiated
promising democratization experiments during the Third Wave, but were unable to sustain democratic
progress, present recurrent key characteristics that were all subsumed under five of the six factors
discussed above: (I) they tend to be poor or lower-middle income countries; (2) they rank low on the
World Bank's good governance scale; (3) they proved particularly ineffective at controlling corruption,
at preventing abuse of executive power, and at building an independent civil service; (4) they suffer from
low capacities when it comes to policy formulation and implementation; and (5) they are deeply split
along ethnic and other lines, often having suffered high levels political violence as a result. 99
A review of the evidence shows that the impact of multiple structural disadvantages -- and, conversely,
of multiple structural advantages -- is particularly strong with regard to hybrid regimes. Hybrid regimes
handicapped by multiple structural disadvantages are far more likely to see democratization falter than
those blessed with multiple structural advantages. One should note, however, that under autocracies
structural conditions come into play in very different, and somewhat perverse, ways. The key point,
here, is that multiple structural advantages appear to facilitate authoritarian consolidation: autocracies
that feature high per-capita income and homogenous populations, and that are well-governed (say, the
UAE), face markedly higher survival prospects than those that do not. 100
Ultimately, when seeking to assess the overall impact of structural conditions on democratic prospects
in hybrid regimes, it may be useful to differentiate among three categories of countries:
• Those with multiple structural disadvantages, where the odds of successful democratization are
extremely low.
• Those with uniformly positive structural conditions, where the odds of successful democratization
are much higher.
• Those in which structural conditions are mixed. At best, countries in that category will face
significant hurdles in their quest for democracy. Evidence suggests that even hybrid-regime countries

ADDITIONAL VARIABLES TO CONSIDER
While among all structural conditions the six factors discussed above may be most decisive in shaping a
country's democratization trajectory, they are not the only ones that might need to receive
consideration during Step Two of the proposed analysis. Among other variables, four deserve particular
mention: the caliber of leadership, the size and autonomy of the middle class, the level of party-system
institutionalization, and the quality of governance in the non-governmental sector.
Caliber of Leadership
Political leadership repeatedly has had a decisive impact on the longer-term trajectory of countries that
experienced a democratic opening. One only needs to think of the contribution of Nelson Mandela (and
F.W. de Klerk) to South Africa's transition, which might have taken a very different turn if the respective
leaders had been very different and unwilling to craft a solution to the country's tensions. Conversely, of
course, leaders bent on undermining democracy (e.g., Hugo Chávez or Alberto Fujimori) played a
significant role in the democratic recession that their respective countries experienced. And, just like
historical legacies, this variable, too, often impacts the six structural conditions discussed earlier. For
instance, whether identity divisions can be successfully accommodated within a democratic framework
is, in part, a function of the readiness and capacities of top leaders to act accordingly (or to thwart that
process). In plural societies, leaders often have played a vital role in the construction of a shared sense
of national identity. But it is not just discrete individuals who matter, but rather the depth and breadth
of the commitment to liberal democratic values across the elite and among senior decision-makers.
While generalizing about a country's "leadership" is inherently difficult and certainly risky, it is hard to
ignore the fact that some countries are better endowed than others when it comes to leadership with
the will and skills to increase the odds of democratic success. In countries where elites appear to be
hopelessly and uniformly corrupt and indifferent or inimical to democracy, democratization may not
stand a fair chance. In contrast, countries that display a critical mass of leaders ready to stand up and
fight for democracy may face better odds. A recent study of what the authors label "democracy's near
misses" is particularly revealing in this regard, 1o2 "Near misses" were defined as two types of scenarios:
instances in which democracy was challenged by forces hostile to it, including majoritarian actors, but
was able to prevail; and cases in which democracy came under threat, regressed, sometimes into

Size and Autonomy of the Middle Class
A growing middle class has long been identified as a crucial force behind democratic change. Historically,
as the middle class has expanded, so often has the demand for freedom, accountability and the rule of
law. Conversely, societies with tiny middle classes have proven to be inhospitable environments for
democratic development. In addition, the size of the middle class can be critical to democratic stability,
in part because as John Maynard Keynes observed nearly a century ago middle-class consumption drives
economic growth (which in turn facilitates democracy), and in part because the middle class often (not
always) contributes to the public sphere attitudes and values generally supportive of democracy. Finally,
while an authoritarian regime may significantly inhibit even a growing middle class's ability to push for
democracy, once the constraints created by that regime are relaxed or lifted, a sizable middle class may
prove to be a powerful asset in advancing and sustaining democratization. Similar dynamics may be at
play if a middle class is willing to tolerate an authoritarian regime not just because of the latter's
coercive powers, but because it also is viewed as critical to ensuring stability and delivering prosperity.
Once perceived threats to stability recede, or if the regime stumbles in its ability to provide for
economic growth, the democratization potential associated with a robust middle class may come into
play.
Therefore, when evaluating the likelihood that a democratic opening may evolve into a consolidated
democracy, the size of the middle class deserves some attention. But the degree of economic
independence of that middle class matters as much as its size. As noted earlier, where the middle class is
dependent on state employment and other state-controlled benefits, and/or when it is enmeshed in
clientelist networks that lead back to the ruling coalition, its ability to act as a democratizing agent is
usually limited. That is why, for instance, the significant expansion of the middle class across the Arab
world from the 1950s through the 1990s did not translate into democratic currents strong enough to
pose a credible challenge to authoritarian regimes.
Finally, onemay note that the size of the middle class is closely tied to the first factor analyzed above,
per capita income, but is not identical to it. A middle class grows out of steadily improving economic
performance and prosperity, but it can exist in a poor country (though in that case it is certainly small
and dependent on support from, or complicity with, ruling elites rather than its own achievements).
Conversely, a country with high per capita GDP can have a small or insignificant middle class if its
economic resources are concentrated in relatively few hands, i.e., if it has high level of economic
inequality and a high Gini coefficient, or if its high GDP is dependent on resources in the hands of an
authoritarian government and ruling class, as is often the case in countries whose GDP is derived
primarily from resource extraction. Yet by and large, as per capita income increases, so often does the
size of the middle class - though not necessarily the extent to which it is politically and economically
independent enough to act as a lever for democracy.
Level of Party-System Institutionalization
The extent to which a country features robust democratic parties operating within an institutionalized
party system is widely recognized as critical to democratic stability. Parties perform critical democracy-
supportive functions, many of which cannot be discharged by other organizations (including those of civil
society). Above all, they aggregate societal interests and political demands, enabling voters to choose

parties, and if elections are to result in democratic outcomes, democratic parties must be strong enough

identifying future leaders and preparing them to assume key political and governing roles; facilitating

representation of constituent interests in legislative bodies and other decision-making arenas. It is
noteworthy as well that party leaders have been preeminent protagonists in most democratic
transitions, while, conversely, anti-democratic parties or the failings of pro-democracy ones have

For parties to play their democracy-supporting roles, however, they must operate within a party system
that is sufficiently institutionalized, and therefore reasonably stable over time. An institutionalized party
system, which may be defined as "one in which a stable set of parties interact regularly in stable ways," 04
provides key political actors as well as the public at large with reasonable guarantees that the rules that
govern political competition and the behavior of key political actors will continue to prevail in the
foreseeable future; those expectations, in turn, support the level of trust in elite interaction and
predictability of political patterns that are needed to sustain democratic life. 105 In contrast, party systems
that are in constant flux -- those in which new parties continuously emerge, but without being able to
solidify, while others frequently disappear or become marginalized, and/or those in which parties
constantly change their policy or ideological positions -- do not provide for the level of consistency and
predictability that voters expect; that enable political actors to have reasonable clear and stable
expectations about their competitors' likely behavior; and that facilitate effective governance.

initially developed in the context of Latin America, has proven highly relevant to accounting for the
democratization trajectories of countries in Africa, Asia, Central Asia and the Middle East, and in
particular for the travails of democracy there. 106 Many of these countries' experiences confirm that

Governance by Non-Government Entities
Factor 3 above underscored that a country's ability to sustain democratic trends is significantly affected
by the performance and effectiveness of its government, and more broadly by state capacity issues. But
a country's broader governance capacities - those that relate to non-governmental actors -- also should
be taken into consideration. For instance, the quality of governance in the civil-society sector is likely to
affect the likelihood that broad civic coalitions able to initiate and sustain democratic momentum will
emerge, or that civil society will be able to push back against authoritarian reassertion efforts and other
backsliding dynamics. Concurrently, effective governance at the grassroots level through interlocking
networks of formal and informal organizations may be critical to relaying the voices of otherwise
marginalized communities, and to ensuring that democratization will take their aspirations and interests
into account, instead of remaining an elite affair. Similarly, the quality of governance in the private sector
may affect prospects for successful democratization both directly (e.g., by strengthening independent
political voices in the private sector) and indirectly (through its impact on economic growth). Thus,
while the most critical dimensions of institutional performance and effectiveness are those that relate to
the government (Factor 3), a country's broader governance capacities also will affect its democratization
trajectory.

BROADER CONSIDERATIONS
However accurate predictions of democratic openings might become, they would still be far from
dispositive about the countries in which USAID should place its democracy attention and resources.
First, the data-driven indices might achieve better than random predictions about the likelihood of
a democratic opening, but they cannot (yet) tell when and, more important, why, they occur. Both
are important for the allocation of democracy resources. A deeper understanding of the socio-political
dynamics of the country should temper the statistically based forecasts, and quite possibly even lead or
override them. And they should certainly inform the allocation and mix of resources between
democracy sub-sectors like political contestation by political parties, legislatures, the rule of law,
independent media, or civil society more generally. Moreover, if a country's democratic opening is far-
distant, it may not be wise to expend substantial resources in that country currently. The decision
would depend on the extentto which that country could reach its opening absent USAID resources or
with modest ones. If the investment of current resources is critical even to a distant opening, perhaps
that investment should be made now notwithstanding the distant returns especially if the country has
substantial geopolitical importance to the United States. Which sector should be prioritized and what
kinds of programs? Which actors and with what interest? The qualitative analysis should help illuminate
the answers to these critical questions.
The level of DRG resources, funding and personnel will also affect the allocation of those resources and
the timeframe for achieving results and development outcomes. A DRG-rich Mission can afford to take
more risks and take a longer time perspective for achieving results. A resource-poor Mission has fewer
options for experimentation and is almost always under more pressure for sooner returns on its
investments.
Second, beyond the probability of a democratic opening and its morphology, lies its significance for
democracy more broadly. To what extent would a successful democratic opening in the country create
a democratic pull, like a gravitational pull, on other countries? What impact would it have on the
trajectory of other countries? What about the reverse? As already noted, Spain and Portugal
inaugurated the Third Wave of democracy in Europe and even in Asia, and much has been written on
the effect of China and Russia on the global expansion of authoritarian regimes and on the democratic
recession. If the Arab Spring had resulted in consolidated democracies rather than a return to
authoritarianism, if, in particular, Egypt's brief fling with democracy had endured and deepened, the
entire Middle East, including the Gulf State might be different today. Conversely the democratic
successes of Costa Rico, Mongolia, Namibia, Moldova, and San Marino had little substantial weight in
their respective regions, let alone globally. USAID should consider the respective implications of
success or failure of various democratic openings in the allocation of its attention and financial
resources. How much of a demonstration effect will a democratic success have on the region? Thus the
statistical significance and probability of a democratic opening is the beginning but not the end for
deciding which democratic openings are politically, not just statistically, significant and where DRG
resources are best invested
